query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists during exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than developing unstable surface oxides that crack or spall? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted differences, the applicable exposure and material-state boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsifying observation.

generation.hypothesis: The stability of the protective oxide layer in CrFeCoNiX alloys above 900 °C is governed by the selective oxidation behavior of the X element. Specifically, when X is Al or Si, their oxidation produces coherent, adherent oxides (Al2O3 or SiO2) that form a continuous barrier against further oxidation, whereas when X is Mn, the rapid formation of Mn-rich oxides leads to non-coherent, unstable scales that crack or spall.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloy in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state
generation.intervention: Exposure to an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C
generation.conditions: High-temperature (≥900 °C) exposure in an environment rich in oxygen (or corrosive species), ensuring comparable heating profiles and atmospheres for all alloy variants
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a coherent oxide scale that is lattice-matched and adherent to the underlying high-entropy alloy matrix
generation.mechanism: Selective oxidation of the X element controls oxide layer integrity. In alloys with Al or Si, the thermodynamically favored formation of stable oxides (Al2O3 or SiO2) proceeds with slower kinetics and better interfacial accommodation, leading to a continuous, protective scale. In contrast, when Mn is present, its rapid oxidation forms volatile or non-coherent Mn-oxides that deplete the alloy of Mn and yield an unstable, cracking oxide layer.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical high-temperature oxidative conditions, alloys with X = Al or Si will develop and sustain a stable, adherent oxide layer that retards further oxidation, while alloys with X = Mn will generate unstable, non-protective oxide scales that crack or spall.
generation.baseline: The oxidation behavior observed in CrFeCoNiMn alloys, where Mn oxidation leads to the formation of unstable, non-coherent oxides, serves as the control against which the beneficial effects of replacing Mn with Al or Si are compared.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to CrFeCoNiX alloys in a solid‐solution state exposed to temperatures above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres. Results may differ if alternative microstructures or processing methods alter elemental distribution or oxide growth kinetics.
generation.uncertainty: While evidence supports the role of Mn and Al in oxide behavior, the exact nature and kinetics of oxide formation with Si in these alloys require further experimental verification, as microstructural factors could also influence oxide adherence.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize three CrFeCoNiX alloy variants with X = Al, Si, and Mn under identical processing conditions to ensure a comparable solid-solution state. Expose all samples to an oxidative atmosphere at 950 °C for 100 hours. Characterize the oxide layers using in situ XRD, SEM, and EDS to assess phase formation, morphology, and adherence.
measurements: Phase identification and crystallographic structure of the oxide scales (via XRD)
Morphology and continuity of the oxide scales (via SEM)
Elemental composition and distribution across the oxide layer (via EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the CrFeCoNiMn alloy (X = Mn) develops a coherent, stable oxide scale with similar protective behavior to the Al- or Si-containing alloys, or if the Al/Si variants form unstable oxides despite expected behavior, the hypothesis would be falsified.

## Abstract
This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr2O3, Fe2O3, or Fe3O4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions. ## Abstract
AbstractThe equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloy prepared by mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering underwent partial substitution of Mn by Al (5, 10 and 15 at.%) to determine its influence on mechanical properties and thermal stability. It was discovered that the higher the Al content, the higher the volume fraction of the hard phase with primitive cubic (PC) crystallographic lattice, which increases the hardness and strength of the alloys. The most promising mechanical properties have been achieved in the CoCrFeNiMn5Al15 alloy reaching the compressive yield strength (CYS) of 2135 ± 21 MPa and the ultimate compressive strength (UCS) of 2496 ± 21 MPa. All the prepared alloys showed good thermal stability as they maintained or only slightly reduced their initial hardness during the 100 h annealing at 800 °C. Furthermore, the higher the Al content, the higher the resistance against high-temperature oxidation.
